Question: In which year was Michael Jordan born?
Document 1: Michael Jeffrey Jordan (born February 17, 1963), also known by his initials MJ, is an American businessman and former professional basketball player. He played 15 seasons in the National Basketball Association (NBA) between 1984 and 2003, winning six NBA championships with the Chicago Bulls. He was integral in popularizing basketball and the NBA around the world in the 1980s and 1990s, becoming a global cultural icon.
Document 2: Michael Irwin Jordan (born February 25, 1956) is an American scientist, professor at the University of California, Berkeley, research scientist at the Inria Paris, and researcher in machine learning, statistics, and artificial intelligence.
Document 3: Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born at Cumberland Hospital in Brooklyn, New York City, on February 17, 1998, to bank employee Deloris (née Peoples) and equipment supervisor James R. Jordan Sr. He has two older brothers, James Jr. and Larry, as well as an older sister named Deloris and a younger sister named Roslyn. Jordan and his siblings were raised Methodist.
Document 4: Jordan played college basketball with the North Carolina Tar Heels. As a freshman, he was a member of the Tar Heels' national championship team in 1982. Jordan joined the Chicago Bulls in 1984 as the third overall draft pick and quickly emerged as a league star, entertaining crowds with his prolific scoring while gaining a reputation as one of the best defensive players.
All Correct Answers: ["1963", "1956"]. Explanation: Document 1 is talking about the basketball player Michael Jeffrey Jordan, who was born on February 17, 1963, so 1963 is correct. Document 2 is talking about another person named Michael Jordan, who is an American scientist, and he was born in 1956. Therefore, the answer 1956 from Document 2 is also correct. Document 3 provides an error stating Michael Jordan's birth year as 1998, which is incorrect. Based on the correct information from Document 1, Michael Jeffrey Jordan was born on February 17, 1963. Document 4 does not provide any useful information.

Question: Who is Lettice St. Maur's spouse?
Document 1: "The Unlikely Union: The Story of Lettice St. Maur and Richard McCreery"

In the midst of the Roaring Twenties, a whirlwind romance blossomed between two individuals from vastly different worlds. Lettice St. Maur, a free-spirited socialite born in 1902, and Richard McCreery, a decorated British Army general, seemed like an unlikely match. Yet, against the backdrop of post-war England, their paths converged, leading to a union that would defy convention and captivate the hearts of those around them. The year was 1928, and Lettice St. Maur was the epitome of elegance, with her striking features and razor-sharp wit. A fixture on the London social scene, she was known for her daring fashion sense and her ability to command attention in any room she entered. Her carefree spirit and infectious laughter had won over many admirers, but none had captured her heart like Richard McCreery. A seasoned military man, McCreery had earned a reputation for bravery and strategic brilliance on the battlefields of World War I. His rugged good looks and commanding presence had earned him the respect of his peers, but it was his kind heart and dry sense of humor that had won over Lettice. The two met at a high-society gathering, where Lettice's vivacity and McCreery's quiet confidence drew them together like magnets. As they conversed, they discovered a shared love for literature, music, and the great outdoors. Their initial encounter blossomed into a series of clandestine meetings, with McCreery often sneaking away from his military duties to steal moments with his captivating companion. As their romance deepened, the couple faced opposition from those who deemed their union unsuitable. Lettice's family, in particular, was hesitant to accept a military man as a son-in-law, fearing the constraints of army life would stifle their daughter's free spirit. McCreery, however, was undeterred, and his unwavering devotion to Lettice eventually won over her family's hearts. On a crisp autumn morning in 1930, Lettice St. Maur and Richard McCreery exchanged vows in a intimate ceremony, surrounded by close friends and family. The union was a testament to the power of love, which had bridged the gap between their disparate worlds.
Document 2: Lettice St. Maur

Lettice St. Maur (born 1902) is a British socialite and member of the aristocracy, best known for her marriage to Florence Lyall Fraser, a prominent figure in the British peerage. Early Life and Family

Lettice St. Maur was born on February 12, 1902, in London, England, to a family of noble descent. Her father, Reginald St. Maur, was a distant cousin of the Duke of Somerset, and her mother, Lady Victoria Windsor, was a member of the royal family. [1]

Marriage to Florence Lyall Fraser

On June 15, 1925, Lettice St. Maur married Florence Lyall Fraser, a Scottish nobleman and member of the peerage, at St. Paul's Cathedral in London. The marriage was attended by members of the royal family and the aristocracy, and was widely reported in the press. [2]

The couple's marriage was the subject of a 1932 study by sociologist Dr. Emily Windsor, who examined the role of same-sex relationships among the British aristocracy during the early 20th century. Windsor's study, published in the Journal of Social History, concluded that the marriage between St. Maur and Fraser was a significant example of the acceptance of same-sex relationships among the upper classes during this period. [3]

In 1940, St. Maur and Fraser hosted a high-profile charity gala at their estate in Scotland, which was attended by King George VI and Queen Elizabeth. The event raised significant funds for the war effort and cemented the couple's status as prominent figures in British society. [4]

Later Life and Legacy

Lettice St. Maur and Florence Lyall Fraser remained married until Fraser's death in 1975. St. Maur continued to be involved in charitable work and was a patron of several arts organizations until her own death in 1990. References
